title: Do Nows: Small Tweaks That Make a Big Difference https://classteaching.wordpress.com/2025/10/17/do-nows-small-tweaks-that-make-a-big-difference/
author: Jody Chan
summary: Jody Chan describes how Do Nows -- already a well-established routine at Durrington High -- became the school's first whole-school teaching focus of the year, chosen because a seemingly embedded practice still showed real variability across departments in question quality, student completion, and student understanding of purpose. She details the fixes adopted for each problem: questions written and discussed collectively during Subject Pedagogy sessions, deliberately mixing recent and older content so no single missed lesson leaves a student unable to answer anything, and calibrating difficulty to start easy and build up; a manageable number of questions (around five) with a set time limit, live marking, and holding students accountable for attempting every question even with just one word; and shared department language explaining to students why and how Do Nows should be completed, delivered in complete silence at the back of exercise books. She closes by describing how she personally adapted her own long-standing Do Now practice, now writing fresh questions each year tailored to each class's specific gaps rather than reusing the same set annually.
points: Chan's framing choice is notable: Do Nows were already universal and "embedded" at her school, yet still became the first whole-school focus, because embedded practice and well-executed practice turned out to be different things.

Her three identified problems -- question quality, completion rates, and student understanding of purpose -- map onto three distinct fixes: collaborative question-writing in Subject Pedagogy sessions, a capped and time-boxed question count with live marking, and shared department language explaining the routine's purpose to students.

The completion-rate fix includes a specific anti-gaming detail: not revealing the lesson title until after the Do Now, so students focus on the questions rather than performatively copying down a title to look busy.

Chan's personal reflection is candid: despite doing Do Nows since before the term existed, she realised she had been reusing the same annual question set rather than tailoring it to each new class's specific gaps, and has since changed that practice.
quotes: At the start of every lesson, she would give her students approximately 10 questions to answer, based on prior learning. She taught me to same, so it is something I have been doing with my classes for a very long time.
While Do Now tasks do have a role in creating a calm and settled start to lessons they can, and should, be so much more than this.
It is important that not all of the questions relate to one lesson, as if a student missed that they will not be able to answer any of the questions.
If there are 15 questions and students routinely only have time to complete 5, we are telling them they don’t need to do all the work we set.
Also, consider not giving them the title until after the do now so that they focus solely on your questions, rather than attempting to be seen writing by studiously copying down the title.
I realised I often used to same questions when teaching a particular topic each year. This meant I was not tailoring it to the needs of my class that year.
